title: Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman (1982)
summary: A tester who is given false information about housing availability suffers an injury under the Fair Housing Act, and an organization whose counseling and referral work is impaired by discrimination has standing in its own right.
notes:
Key line: "A tester who has been the object of a misrepresentation made unlawful under § 804(d) has suffered injury in precisely the form the statute was intended to guard against, and therefore has standing to maintain a claim for damages under the Act's provisions." Justice Brennan, for the Court.

Citation: 455 U.S. 363 (1982).

sections.Parties: Petitioners were Havens Realty Corp., which owned and operated the Camelot Townhouses and Colonial Court Apartments in Henrico County, Virginia, a suburb of Richmond, and Rose Jones, one of its employees. Respondents were Sylvia Coleman, a Black tester; R. Kent Willis, a white tester; and Housing Opportunities Made Equal (HOME), a nonprofit corporation whose purpose was to make equal opportunity in housing a reality in the Richmond area and which employed the testers. Paul Coles, a Black renter, was also a plaintiff, but his claims were resolved separately. The respondents sued for damages and injunctive relief under section 812 of the Fair Housing Act of 1968.
sections.Material Facts: Testers are people who pose as renters to collect evidence of unlawful steering. On March 14 and July 13, 1978, Coleman asked Havens about apartment availability and was told none were available, while on the same days Willis was told that vacancies existed. Coles, a Black renter who actually sought housing, was told on July 13, 1978 that no apartments were available. The complaint alleged that Havens's steering practices deprived the individual plaintiffs, who lived in Richmond or Henrico County, of the benefits of living in an integrated community, and that the practices frustrated HOME's counseling and referral services and drained its resources. Section 804(d) of the Act makes it unlawful to represent to any person because of race that a dwelling is unavailable when it is available. Suit was filed on January 9, 1979, within 180 days of the July incidents but more than 180 days after the March incidents.
sections.Procedural History: The District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia dismissed the claims of Coleman, Willis and HOME, holding that they lacked standing and that some claims were barred by the 180-day limitations period. Coles's claims proceeded to trial, and Havens was found to have engaged in unlawful steering. The Fourth Circuit reversed the dismissal, holding that the allegations sufficed at the pleading stage and that a continuing violation brought the earlier acts within the limitations period. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and on February 24, 1982 affirmed in part and reversed in part.
sections.Issue: Section 812 of the Fair Housing Act authorizes suit by any person who claims to have been injured by a discriminatory housing practice, and Gladstone had held that Congress extended standing under that section to the limits of Article III. The plaintiffs included a tester who was lied to, a tester who was told the truth, residents of the metropolitan area, and a fair housing organization. Do a tester who received false information, a tester who received accurate information, residents claiming loss of the benefits of an integrated community, and an organization claiming a drain on its resources each have Article III standing to sue under section 812?
sections.Holding: Coleman has standing as a tester because section 804(d) gives any person a right to truthful housing information and a misrepresentation to her is the precise injury the statute guards against, even though she expected false information and did not intend to rent. Willis lacks tester standing because he received accurate information. The neighborhood claims survive dismissal pending proof that the plaintiffs lived where the steering had an appreciable effect. HOME has standing in its own right because impairment of its counseling and referral services and the drain on its resources is a concrete injury.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Brennan relied on Gladstone, Realtors v. Village of Bellwood, which held that Congress extended standing under section 812 to the full limits of Article III, so the only question was injury in fact. Section 804(d) creates a legal right to truthful information about housing availability. A tester who is lied to has suffered the invasion of that right, and Article III does not care that the tester planned the encounter or had no intention of renting; Congress may create legal rights whose invasion constitutes injury. Willis received truthful information and so had no statutory injury and no cause of action under section 804(d). On the neighborhood claims, the Court found it implausible that steering at two apartment complexes could affect the whole Richmond area, but held that at the pleading stage the plaintiffs might prove they lived in a neighborhood where the practices had a real effect. On HOME's claim, the Court held that an organization suffers injury in fact when a defendant's conduct perceptibly impairs its ability to provide services and forces it to devote resources to counteract the discrimination; that harm is concrete and goes beyond an abstract setback to its social interests. The Court also held that a continuing violation brings earlier acts within the 180-day filing period so long as the last act falls within the period.

learning.separateOpinions: The judgment was unanimous, 9 to 0. Justice Powell concurred, joined by Justice Rehnquist and Justice O'Connor, stressing that the neighborhood claims would fail unless the plaintiffs proved they lived in a relatively compact area affected by the steering, since Richmond and Henrico County cover about 269 square miles with about 390,000 residents, and warning that Article III must not be satisfied by meaningless pleading.
